scenes.label: Meet the team
scenes.title: A polished paragraph
scenes.caption: For the science magazine, Dev reviews a fictional assistant response about the school garden. It confidently says every seed needs sunlight to germinate and cites a booklet page.
scenes.dialogue: Fluent writing can still be wrong.

scenes.label: The problem
scenes.title: Open the source
scenes.caption: The supplied booklet extract says seed requirements vary and describes moisture, suitable temperature and air for the examples discussed. Its quoted page does not support the universal sunlight claim.

scenes.label: How it works
scenes.title: What generation does
scenes.caption: The teacher explains that language models generate plausible continuations using patterns learned during training. A confident tone is not a built in fact check. Dev marks which statements the supplied extract supports and which require another trustworthy source before the class can publish them.

scenes.label: Your decision
scenes.title: Choose an editorial action
scenes.caption: The team can publish unchanged, invent a better looking reference or revise the sentence to match the available evidence. Choose a response that keeps uncertainty visible.

scenes.label: What changes
scenes.title: Credit and responsibility
scenes.caption: Dev revises the paragraph and records that a simulated assistant draft was checked and edited by students. The teacher reviews the final science explanation. The team avoids claiming the assistant conducted an experiment, and it keeps names, private messages and unpublished personal details out of requests.

scenes.label: Enter the lab
scenes.title: A changed claim
scenes.caption: Another draft claims a particular fertiliser always doubles growth. The supplied card reports only one small fictional trial. In the lab, check each claim, prepare a cautious revision and write a safe request that asks for evidence and limitations rather than unsupported certainty.
